screens.title: Error Handling and Events
screens.subtitle: When to use require, revert and assert — custom errors and emit for off-chain observability

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn how Solidity signals problems and how contracts communicate with the outside world. We cover the three built-in error mechanisms — require, revert, and assert — and explain why each exists, how gas behavior differs between them, and the practical consequences for security. You'll also see custom errors, a Solidity 0.8.4 feature that reduces gas and carries structured data when reverting. Finally, we'll cover events and the emit keyword: events let contracts publish logs that off-chain systems can query efficiently, and indexing parameters makes those logs searchable. This chapter matters because error handling affects both safety and user cost: using the wrong primitive can waste gas or mask a critical bug. As an example, input validation should use require so users get unused gas refunded, while invariants belong to assert to flag impossible states. Throughout the lesson we will inspect example contracts, walk through a voting contract that uses custom errors and events, and give practical rules of thumb you can apply immediately. By the end, you'll know which mechanism to pick, how to structure custom errors, and how to design events that are easy to filter and parse.

keyIdea.title: Chapter focus
keyIdea.text: Choose require/revert for expected failures and refunds, use assert for invariants, prefer custom errors to save gas, and emit indexed events for efficient off-chain queries.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of these lessons you will be able to pick the correct Solidity error primitive for common situations, explain how gas behaves when a transaction fails, and implement custom errors to reduce gas and provide structured failure data. You will also be able to declare and emit events, choose which parameters to index, and design logs that off-chain clients can query efficiently. For example, you will use require to validate user inputs and permissions so users receive unused gas back when calls fail. You will use assert only to check invariants that indicate a bug if violated. You will define custom errors when a structured error payload is useful and gas budget matters. Finally, you will add emit statements and index the most commonly filtered addresses to make your contract observable by block explorers and front-end listeners. These skills improve contract resilience, save gas for users, and make your contract easier to monitor and debug in production.

narration.text: These objectives focus on applying error handling and event design in real contracts and tests. You will instrument contracts with require and revert for expected errors, and write assert checks only for internal invariants. You will replace long error strings with custom errors when transaction size or gas matters, and you will emit events with indexed parameters that front-ends can filter efficiently. Practically, you'll implement a voting contract that uses a custom AlreadyVoted error and emits VoteCast with an indexed voter address so explorers can find votes quickly. In testing, you will assert that functions revert under invalid conditions and confirm that custom error data matches expectations. Mastery means choosing the least-gas, clearest pattern that preserves observability and signals real bugs versus user mistakes.

screens.title: require(): Validate inputs and permissions
screens.subtitle: Use require for expected preconditions and refunding remaining gas

narration.text: Require is the primary guard you will use to check conditions that must hold before a function proceeds. It accepts a boolean condition and an optional error message. When the condition is false, the call reverts, state changes are rolled back, and the transaction refunds any remaining gas. This makes require appropriate for input validation and permission checks, such as ensuring a caller is the contract owner or that an amount is positive. A practical example is verifying msg. sender equals owner before changing a state variable. Using require clearly communicates that a failure is an expected outcome caused by user input, not a contract bug. A common misconception is to reserve require only for simple checks; in fact require is also fine inside modifiers and for early exits in more complex flows. Avoid using long error strings when gas is tight; later we'll show how custom errors provide structured, cheaper alternatives. Key takeaway: use require for predictable, user-caused failures so the caller gets unused gas back. Can you spot which input checks in your contracts should be require guards and which are invariants that belong in assert?

keyIdea.title: Use require for expected failures
keyIdea.text: require reverts and refunds remaining gas; ideal for input validation and permission checks.

content.html:
Core Concept
require()
Validate preconditions and permissions. Failing require reverts and refunds unused gas.
When to use
  • Input validation (e.g., amount > 0)
  • Access control checks (owner-only functions)
  • Sanity checks on parameters before state changes
Example
function setValue(uint256 _newValue) public {
  require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can set value.");
  require(_newValue > 0, "New value must be greater than zero.");
  value = _newValue;
}
Key Takeaway

Use require for expected input or permission failures so callers are refunded unused gas.

Illustration & Common Mistakes
Correct
Checking caller address and positive amounts with require. These are expected user errors.
Common Mistake
Using require for invariants that indicate a logic bug. Prefer assert for those.
Quick checklist
  • Is this a user input or permission check? Use require.
  • Do I want the caller refunded for unused gas if it fails? Yes → require.
  • Keep error messages concise; later replace with custom errors when needed.

screens.title: revert(): Explicit rollback with flexible logic
screens.subtitle: Use revert in complex conditionals and to centralize error handling

narration.text: Revert is a statement you use when an explicit rollback is required from complex logic branches. It behaves like require in that it reverts state changes and refunds remaining gas, but it is often used when you need conditional checks inside nested logic rather than a single boolean expression. Because require is syntactic sugar for an if-not-revert pattern, revert provides clearer control for multiple paths. For example, you might check complex eligibility rules and call revert with a specific message or a custom error when multiple conditions fail. Revert is also helpful to centralize error handling in a helper function that validates several invariants and reverts with a targeted message. A misconception is thinking revert is more expensive than require — gas behavior for refunding is the same; the difference is clarity and where you place the check. Key takeaway: prefer require for single precondition checks and revert when branching logic or centralized rollback improves readability and maintainability. revert(): Explicit rollback with flexible logic means revert rolls back state and refunds gas; use it for complex conditionals or centralized checks where require is awkward.. In practical terms, use revert in complex conditionals and to centralize error handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use revert for flexible rollbacks
keyIdea.text: revert rolls back state and refunds gas; use it for complex conditionals or centralized checks where require is awkward.

content.html:
Core Concept
revert()
Explicitly revert with flexible logic and conditional checks. Refunds remaining gas like require.
Example
function withdraw(uint256 _amount) public {
  if (_amount == 0) {
    revert("Withdrawal amount cannot be zero.");
  }
  if (_amount > value) {
    revert("Insufficient contract balance.");
  }
  value -= _amount;
}
When to prefer revert
  • Multiple conditional branches where each branch returns a different reason.
  • When centralizing validation into helper functions that call revert on failure.
  • When you need a targeted rollback deeper inside function logic rather than at entrance.
Misconception
revert is not inherently costlier than require; use the one that makes code clearer while still refunding unused gas on failure.
Key Takeaway

Use revert when branching or centralized rollback increases clarity; it refunds gas like require.

screens.title: assert(): Guard invariants, flag bugs
screens.subtitle: Use assert only for conditions that should never be false

narration.text: Assert is a stronger primitive intended to check internal invariants — conditions that should never occur if the contract logic is correct. When assert fails it reverts and consumes all remaining gas without refund. This behavior intentionally makes assert failures costly and obvious, signaling a serious bug or corrupted state. Typical uses include verifying internal accounting invariants or properties that should hold after complex updates, for instance asserting that the sum of balances equals total supply. A common error is using assert for ordinary input validation; that both misrepresents the failure type and increases cost because users lose remaining gas. Another misconception is thinking assert prevents exploits; it only signals them at runtime and halts the transaction. The safe rule is: use assert for invariants and sanity checks that indicate a developer error if violated, and use require or revert for user-caused or expected errors. This distinction helps auditors and tools interpret failures and improves responsible error semantics in your contracts. assert(): Guard invariants, flag bugs means assert indicates impossible states; failures consume all remaining gas and signal bugs rather than user errors.. In practical terms, use assert only for conditions that should never be false. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Assert for invariants
keyIdea.text: assert indicates impossible states; failures consume all remaining gas and signal bugs rather than user errors.

content.html:
Core Concept
assert()
Verify invariants and internal consistency. On failure, all remaining gas is consumed.
Example
// After transfers, total supply should equal sum of balances
assert(balanceOf[address(this)] == totalSupply);
Why assert is special
  • Signals a developer-level bug rather than a user mistake.
  • Consumes remaining gas on failure to make issues visible and expensive.
  • Useful in post-state checks after complex updates to detect corruption.
Common Mistake
Using assert for input validation or expected user failures. That wastes gas and miscommunicates intent.
Key Takeaway

Reserve assert for impossible internal invariants; use require or revert for user-caused checks.

screens.title: Gas behavior: refunds vs consumed gas
screens.subtitle: How require/revert differ from assert in transaction costs

narration.text: Understanding gas behavior when errors occur is central to designing user-friendly contracts. When require or revert causes a transaction to fail, the EVM reverts state and refunds remaining gas to the caller. This reduces the economic impact of expected user mistakes. In contrast, an assert failure is treated as a critical error and consumes all remaining gas; it leaves no refund. The intent behind this design is to make developer errors visible and costly so they are noticed and fixed. A common practical implication is to avoid using assert for any check that could reasonably result from user input; doing so will make failed user transactions expensive. A concrete example: validating a deposit amount should use require, which refunds leftover gas on failure. Checking that internal balances sum to total supply after transfers should use assert, because a mismatch indicates a deeper bug. When you profile gas, remember that custom errors also reduce the size of revert data and can slightly lower gas used by failed transactions compared to long error strings. The key question to ask is whether the failing condition is a user mistake or a contract invariant — that determines the correct primitive.

keyIdea.title: Gas impact guide
keyIdea.text: require/revert refund remaining gas for expected failures; assert consumes remaining gas to signal critical bugs.

content.html:
Expected failure — require / revert
State is reverted and remaining gas is refunded to the caller. This keeps user cost lower for invalid inputs.
Gas returned on revert
Refunded gas reduces wasted cost for callers who make expected mistakes.
Critical failure — assert
On assert failure the transaction reverts and consumes all remaining gas. This should only happen when logic is broken.
Gas consumed on assert
Use assert to make bugs costly and visible to developers and auditors.
Practical tip
  • Prefer require/revert for user-driven checks to avoid punitive gas costs.
  • Replace long revert strings with custom errors to shrink revert data and save gas.
  • Use assert only for post-state invariants that should never change under correct logic.
Key Takeaway

Pick the primitive based on whether the failure is expected from user input or indicates a bug; gas behavior follows from that choice.

screens.title: Custom Errors (Solidity 0.8.4+)
screens.subtitle: Define and revert with custom error types to save gas and structure data

narration.text: Custom errors let you declare error types and revert with them, carrying structured data instead of long strings. They were introduced in Solidity 0.8.4 to reduce the on-chain cost of revert messages by encoding error identifiers and arguments more compactly. For example, declaring error Unauthorized(address caller) and then reverting Unauthorized(msg. sender) provides an error topic and encoded parameters that off-chain tools can decode. The benefits are twofold: smaller revert payloads reduce gas used when errors occur, and structured data is easier for automated tooling to parse than free-form strings. Use custom errors when you expect frequent reverts, or when you need to return typed data on failure for debugging and tooling. A common pitfall is overusing custom errors for rare, single-use messages — balance readability and gas savings. Remember that custom errors still revert and follow the same gas semantics as revert or require depending on usage. Practically, define errors at contract scope and use them in if-conditions or helper functions to keep code concise and efficient. Custom Errors (Solidity 0.8.4+) means declare custom errors and revert with them to send structured, gas-efficient error data to callers and tools.. In practical terms, define and revert with custom error types to save gas and structure data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Custom errors save gas
keyIdea.text: Declare custom errors and revert with them to send structured, gas-efficient error data to callers and tools.

content.html:
Core Concept
Custom Errors
Define typed error types and revert with them to reduce revert data size and gas.
Declaration
error Unauthorized(address caller);
error InsufficientBalance(uint256 required, uint256 available);
Using a custom error
Revert with structured arguments that off-chain tools can decode from the transaction receipt.
Example
if (msg.sender != owner) {
  revert Unauthorized(msg.sender);
}
if (_amount > balance) {
  revert InsufficientBalance(_amount, balance);
}
Key Takeaway

Use custom errors to reduce gas and provide typed revert data for tooling; define them at contract scope.

screens.title: Custom Error Example: structured reverts
screens.subtitle: See custom errors in practice and their compact encoding

narration.text: Let's walk through a practical custom error example and understand how it encodes data. In the sample contract a pair of errors Unauthorized(address) and InsufficientBalance(uint256,uint256) are declared at the top-level. When a function checks caller identity or balance, it reverts using those errors and passes concrete values as arguments. Off-chain tools receive the error selector and encoded arguments in the transaction's revert data. Because the error selector is a fixed identifier and parameters are typed, the encoded payload is shorter and cheaper than long string messages. A common misconception is that custom errors are only for advanced projects; in fact, they are beneficial anytime you expect frequent reverts or want structured debugging data. Use them in public APIs and for reusable checks in libraries or modifiers. As you test, compare gas for a revert with a long string and a revert with a custom error to see the difference. The takeaway: custom errors give you both clarity and efficiency when used correctly. Custom Error Example: structured reverts means custom errors encode an identifier and typed arguments, producing smaller revert payloads and clearer programmatic data.. In practical terms, see custom errors in practice and their compact encoding. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Custom error walkthrough
keyIdea.text: Custom errors encode an identifier and typed arguments, producing smaller revert payloads and clearer programmatic data.

content.html:
Code Example
// Custom Errors
error Unauthorized(address caller);
error InsufficientBalance(uint256 required, uint256 available);

contract CustomErrorExample {
  uint256 public balance = 100;
  address public owner;

  constructor() {
    owner = msg.sender;
  }

  function doSomething(uint256 _amount) public {
    if (msg.sender != owner) {
      revert Unauthorized(msg.sender);
    }
    if (_amount > balance) {
      revert InsufficientBalance(_amount, balance);
    }
    balance -= _amount;
  }
}
Explanation
  • Errors declared once and reused across functions.
  • Revert passes typed data, which off-chain clients decode deterministically.
  • Gas saved compared to long revert strings because of compact encoding.
Check
Compare gas for revert with string vs custom error in a test to measure savings.

screens.title: Events and emit: communicating off-chain
screens.subtitle: How contracts publish logs that UIs and analytics tools can read

narration.text: Events let contracts write information to transaction logs so external systems can observe contract activity without reading contract storage. You declare events much like a function signature and then use the emit keyword to publish them. Events are stored in the transaction receipt and can be queried by block explorers and off-chain listeners. Because logs are cheaper than storage, events are the recommended way to record occurrences such as transfers, ownership changes, or votes. For example, emitting Transfer(from, to, value) during a token transfer informs front-ends and analytics that a movement occurred. Remember that events do not change contract state and cannot be accessed by other contracts. A common pitfall is trying to rely on events for critical on-chain logic or for security checks — events are for external observers and diagnostics. Design events to include the minimal, relevant data and think about which fields you will need to filter by when deciding which to mark indexed. Events and emit: communicating off-chain means use events and emit to publish off-chain logs; they are cheaper than storage and ideal for uis and analytics.. In practical terms, how contracts publish logs that uis and analytics tools can read. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Emit for logs
keyIdea.text: Use events and emit to publish off-chain logs; they are cheaper than storage and ideal for UIs and analytics.

content.html:
Core Concept
Events & emit
Emit logs to make contract activity discoverable to off-chain systems without using storage.
Example
event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 value);

function transfer(address _to, uint256 _amount) public returns (bool) {
  // transfer logic
  emit Transfer(msg.sender, _to, _amount);
  return true;
}
Design considerations
  • Events are cheap for off-chain observers but not reliable for on-chain decisions.
  • Include the minimal data needed; avoid writing large blobs to logs.
  • Decide which fields will be filtered in UIs and mark them indexed (up to three).
Key Takeaway

Emit concise events and index likely query fields so UIs can efficiently find relevant logs.

screens.title: Indexed parameters: make logs searchable
screens.subtitle: Choose up to three indexed fields that your off-chain clients will filter on

narration.text: Indexing event parameters places them into topics, which are separate, searchable fields in the transaction log. Solidity allows up to three indexed parameters per event. Indexing is essential when you expect off-chain clients to filter logs by specific values like an address or identifier. For example, marking from and to as indexed in a Transfer event enables block explorers to quickly return all transfers for a given address. Non-indexed parameters remain in the data portion of the log and require scanning or decoding each log to find. When you design events, ask which fields will be used as filters by your front-end or analytics pipeline, then index those fields, up to the limit. Over-indexing irrelevant fields wastes topic slots that could be used by others. Remember that indexing only helps off-chain queries; indexed fields are not directly accessible to other contracts. The practical heuristic is: index the most commonly queried fields such as user addresses or token identifiers, and keep the rest as non-indexed data. This balances query performance with compact log payloads. Indexed parameters: make logs searchable means index parameters that front-ends will filter on; up to three fields can be indexed for fast off-chain queries.. In practical terms, choose up to three indexed fields that your off-chain clients will filter on. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Index thoughtfully
keyIdea.text: Index parameters that front-ends will filter on; up to three fields can be indexed for fast off-chain queries.

content.html:
Indexed vs Non-indexed
Indexed parameters appear in topics and are searchable without inspecting the log data. Non-indexed parameters sit in the data blob and require decoding every log to locate values.
Example Event
event VoteCast(address indexed voter, uint256 candidateId); — here voter is indexed so front-ends can quickly find votes by address.
Design checklist
  • Which fields will UIs filter by? Index those first.
  • Keep event payloads small; don't store large strings in logs.
  • Remember the three-index limit and plan events accordingly.
Key Takeaway

Index the most commonly queried fields to make log queries fast and cost-effective for clients.

screens.title: Voting contract walkthrough: errors and events
screens.subtitle: A compact Voting contract that uses require, custom errors, and emits events

narration.text: We'll walk through the Voting contract that combines the chapter patterns. The contract declares custom errors AlreadyVoted(address) and InvalidCandidateId(uint256) and events VoteCast(address indexed voter, uint256 candidateId) and CandidateAdded(uint256 indexed candidateId, string name). addCandidate is guarded by a modifier that uses require to verify the caller is the owner. The vote function uses require to prevent the zero address voter and to validate the candidate exists. It then uses revert AlreadyVoted(msg. sender) to signal repeated voting attempts with structured data. After recording the vote, the contract emits VoteCast with the voter address indexed so front-ends can quickly find a user's votes. This example demonstrates choosing require for expected inputs, custom errors for gas-efficient structured reverts, and events to log state changes for off-chain use. When testing, assert that duplicate voting causes the custom error and that the VoteCast log appears with the correct indexed topic. This pattern keeps on-chain checks clear and off-chain observability straightforward. Voting contract walkthrough: errors and events means combine require for validation, custom errors for repeated conditions, and indexed events to make votes discoverable off-chain.. In practical terms, a compact voting contract that uses require, custom errors, and emits events. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Voting contract pattern
keyIdea.text: Combine require for validation, custom errors for repeated conditions, and indexed events to make votes discoverable off-chain.

content.html:
Key Contract Snippet
// Custom Error
error AlreadyVoted(address voter);
error InvalidCandidateId(uint256 candidateId);

contract Voting {
  address public owner;
  uint256 public nextCandidateId = 0;
  mapping(uint256 => string) public candidates;
  mapping(uint256 => uint256) public voteCounts;
  mapping(address => bool) public hasVoted;

  event VoteCast(address indexed voter, uint256 candidateId);
  event CandidateAdded(uint256 indexed candidateId, string name);

  constructor() { owner = msg.sender; }

  modifier onlyOwner() {
    require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can call this function.");
    _;
  }

  function addCandidate(string memory _name) public onlyOwner {
    candidates[nextCandidateId] = _name;
    emit CandidateAdded(nextCandidateId, _name);
    nextCandidateId++;
  }

  function vote(uint256 _candidateId) public {
    require(msg.sender != address(0), "Voter address cannot be zero.");
    if (hasVoted[msg.sender]) { revert AlreadyVoted(msg.sender); }
    require(_candidateId < nextCandidateId, "Invalid candidate ID.");
    voteCounts[_candidateId]++;
    hasVoted[msg.sender] = true;
    emit VoteCast(msg.sender, _candidateId);
  }
}
Explanation & Testing
  • alreadyVoted is a custom error that returns the voter's address for tooling.
  • VoteCast indexes voter so UIs can filter votes by address efficiently.
  • Tests should assert that duplicate voting reverts with the custom error and that VoteCast appears in the logs.
Key Takeaway

This pattern keeps validation explicit, errors compact and structured, and events searchable for off-chain consumers.

screens.title: Common mistakes, testing and observability
screens.subtitle: Avoid assert misuse, test reverts, and verify events in receipts

narration.text: This screen collects practical best practices and common pitfalls you should watch for. First, never use assert for input validation; it makes user errors costly and confuses intent. Second, write unit tests that expect reverts and custom errors where appropriate; testing both the revert type and emitted event ensures your contract behaviour is observable and correct. Third, when you emit events test that indexed topics contain the expected values — this verifies that front-end queries will succeed. Fourth, prefer custom errors when revert messages are long or when structured data will be parsed by tooling; measure gas impact in tests to justify the change. Fifth, remember events are off-chain logs only; never depend on them for on-chain state transitions or security checks. Finally, document which fields you indexed and why, so integrators know how to query logs. A good practice is to keep a short test that exercises an expected revert, compares gas for string vs custom error, and confirms the event topics. These steps improve reliability and observability in production. Common mistakes, testing and observability means test reverts, prefer custom errors when it saves gas, verify event topics in receipts, and never rely on events for on-chain logic.. In practical terms, avoid assert misuse, test reverts, and verify events in receipts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Testing & observability
keyIdea.text: Test reverts, prefer custom errors when it saves gas, verify event topics in receipts, and never rely on events for on-chain logic.

content.html:
Checklist: Avoid common mistakes
  • Use require/revert for user-driven validations; use assert only for invariants.
  • Write tests that assert specific revert behavior and check custom error arguments.
  • Confirm events are emitted and indexed topics match expected values in receipts.
  • Measure gas difference between long revert strings and custom errors before refactoring.
  • Do not design on-chain logic that depends on events; they are off-chain observability tools.
Pro Tip
Keep a small test suite that intentionally triggers reverts and checks both the revert type and the transaction receipt for events. This prevents regressions and ensures UIs can rely on logs.
Key Takeaway

Testing reverts and events is the best way to ensure your error-handling design works in production and is observable by off-chain systems.

narration.text: Let's summarize the core ideas. Use require for expected preconditions and permission checks so callers receive refunds of unused gas when a call fails. Use revert when you need flexible, conditional rollback logic or centralized validation, remembering it also refunds gas. Reserve assert for internal invariants that should never be false; when assert fails it consumes remaining gas and signals a critical bug. Prefer custom errors to long revert strings when you need structured, gas-efficient failure data. Use events and the emit keyword to publish logs for off-chain systems, and mark up to three parameters as indexed when you expect clients to filter on them. These choices directly affect security, debugging, and user cost. The simplest rule of thumb: expected user errors → require/revert; impossible internal states → assert; structured, frequent failures → custom errors; visibility for UIs → events with indexed fields. Keep these practices in mind as you write and audit contracts.

keyIdea.title: Quick summary
keyIdea.text: Pick the right primitive: require/revert for expected failures, assert for bugs, custom errors for efficiency, and indexed events for observability.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Key Concepts
require()
Use for input and permission checks; refunds remaining gas on failure.
assert()
Use for invariants only; failure consumes remaining gas and signals bugs.
Custom Errors
Declare structured errors and revert with them to save gas and carry typed data.
Events & indexed
Emit logs for off-chain systems. Index up to three fields that clients will filter by to improve query performance.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three essential reminders before you code

narration.text: A short set of practical reminders: validate user inputs with require or revert so callers receive refunds; use assert only for invariants that indicate bugs and accept the gas penalty if they fail; and prefer custom errors when revert messages are long or you need structured revert data to save gas. Also, use events and index parameters that UIs will filter by; never depend on events for on-chain control. Before deploying, add tests that trigger expected reverts, confirm custom error arguments, and verify events appear with the correct topics. These steps reduce user cost, improve debugging, and increase contract observability. Keep these rules as a checklist when you write or audit contracts. What to Remember means require/revert for validation, assert for invariants, custom errors for efficiency, and indexed events for observability — test them all.. In practical terms, three essential reminders before you code. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Final checklist
keyIdea.text: Require/revert for validation, assert for invariants, custom errors for efficiency, and indexed events for observability — test them all.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › What to Remember
01 — Validate with require
Use require for expected input and permission checks so callers are refunded unused gas.
02 — Use assert sparingly
Only check invariants with assert; failures indicate bugs and consume remaining gas.
03 — Emit and index events
Emit concise events and index the fields UIs will filter by to make logs queryable.
Summary Takeaway

Choosing the correct error primitive and designing events carefully improves security, reduces gas costs for users, and makes your contract easier to monitor and maintain.
